modules.title: 1. Financial Meaning, Probability and Statistical Uncertainty
modules.description: Start after Common Foundation. Reuse its Python, SQL, Git, Linux, elementary mathematics and testing skills; do not retake them here. Learn what financial quantities mean and how uncertainty changes the interpretation of observations.

lessons.title: Financial instruments, cash flows and units
objectives: Distinguish ownership, debt and contingent claims without assuming finance vocabulary.
Draw dated cash flows and explain discounting.
Separate prices, quantities, returns, currencies and time horizons.

topics.title: What is being owned or promised?
details: An equity is an ownership claim; a bond promises specified payments subject to credit risk.
A derivative depends on an underlying variable; its payoff is not the same as its purchase price.
A quoted price is not evidence that your order would execute at that price.

topics.title: Money has a date and unit
details: Present value versus future value; rate, compounding frequency and maturity.
Coupon, principal, price and yield are different quantities.
Use fictional currency units and explicit time conventions in all examples.

topics.title: Role boundaries
details: Researchers test hypotheses; developers build reliable financial systems.
Traders/execution specialists manage trading behavior and operational exposure.
Pricing/risk quants need instrument-specific mathematics; this is not a universal HFT curriculum.

video.locator: Lecture 1: Introduction, Financial Terms and Concepts

reading.locator: 7.3 Methods for Solving Time Value of Money Problems; 10.1 Characteristics of Bonds

assignment.title: Create a fictional instrument and cash-flow catalogue
instructions: Define six fictional contracts: equity, zero-coupon bond, coupon bond, forward, European call and interest-rate swap. Write your own descriptions, not copied product specifications.
For each, record units, dates, promised or contingent payments and at least two unresolved risks.
Calculate present values for three independent fixed cash-flow fixtures using a stated annual effective rate; keep derivative valuation out of this first exercise.
deliverables: three hand-calculated fixtures and a small verification notebook
acceptanceCriteria: All six entries identify what determines the payment and whether it is guaranteed by the model, contingent or exposed to default.
Zero-rate discounting leaves nominal cash flows unchanged; a positive discount rate lowers the present value of a fixed positive future payment.
Every number has a currency/unit and date; no current market quote or investment recommendation is included.

questions.prompt: Why can an option's terminal payoff differ from the buyer's overall cash result?
questions.answer: The buyer also paid a premium and may incur financing and transaction costs.
questions.explanation: A payoff describes the contract's terminal payment, not every cash flow associated with acquiring and holding it.

reviewPrompts: How would you explain a bond to someone who only knows database records?
Which parts of an instrument definition are economic assumptions rather than implementation details?

lessons.title: Conditioning, Bayes and probability-weighted outcomes
objectives: Translate a conditional statement into a denominator and eligible population.
Calculate an expectation from a finite probability table.
Explain why rare-event base rates matter when interpreting alerts.

topics.title: Conditional knowledge
details: An event's probability can change after observing other information.
Conditioning restricts the population; it does not establish causation.
Prior probability, likelihood and posterior probability play different roles.

topics.title: Expected values
details: A probability-weighted average need not be an outcome that ever occurs.
Distinguish an expectation from a guarantee and from a single realized observation.
Conditional expectations must be averaged using the probabilities of their conditions.

topics.title: Financial-system interpretation
details: A delayed-data alert can have a high false-alert count when true incidents are rare.
Separate event frequencies from the financial size of consequences.
Document the population on which a quoted probability was estimated.

video.locator: Lecture 2: Conditioning and Bayes' Rule; use Lecture 12: Iterated Expectations for the extension

reading.locator: Chapter 3 Probability Mass Functions, 3.2 Summarizing a PMF; Chapter 13 Survival analysis, 13.1 Survival Functions and 13.2 Hazard Function for an applied conditioning example

assignment.title: Audit a synthetic market-data alert
instructions: Invent a 10,000-message audit table with 100 truly delayed messages, of which 90 are alerted, and 99 alerts among the remaining messages.
Calculate the probability of delay given an alert, the probability of an alert given delay, and the expected review count.
Recalculate using a tenfold higher incident base rate while holding sensitivity and false-positive rate fixed; explain the change in plain language.
acceptanceCriteria: The first case reports 189 alerts and delay-given-alert of 90/189, not 90/100.
All conditional probabilities identify their denominator.
The memo distinguishes an illustrative assumed table from measured operational performance.

questions.prompt: Does an alert that detects 90% of delayed messages imply that 90% of alerts indicate delays?
questions.answer: No. The latter also depends on the delay base rate and false-positive rate.
questions.explanation: The two probabilities condition on different populations.

reviewPrompts: What is lost when someone reports only an alert's sensitivity?
Why is an expectation not a promise about one observation?

lessons.title: Random variables, dependence and reproducible simulation
objectives: Describe a joint distribution and distinguish dependence from marginal behavior.
Estimate means, variances and covariance from synthetic samples.
Use seeded simulation without confusing repeatability with realism.

topics.title: Distributions and moments
details: A random variable maps uncertain outcomes to numbers with defined units.
Mean, variance and covariance answer different questions.
Equal marginal distributions can coexist with different joint risks.

topics.title: Dependence
details: Independence is stronger than zero correlation.
Aggregation can amplify shared shocks instead of diversifying them.
A shuffle destroys some dependence and is valid only under the assumed null.

topics.title: Simulation as a model
details: A pseudorandom seed controls a computational experiment, not market uncertainty.
Monte Carlo error comes from finite sampling; model error comes from incorrect assumptions.
Keep generator parameters and random-number-library versions in the run manifest.

video.locator: Lecture 3: Independence; Lecture 11: Derived Distributions; Convolution; Covariance and Correlation

reading.locator: 7.3 Correlation; 9.4 Testing a Correlation

assignment.title: Compare three synthetic dependence structures
instructions: Generate 5,000 paired observations for three cases: independent zero-mean unit-normal variables, identical variables, and opposite variables.
Keep each marginal distribution comparable and calculate the variance of their sum.
Repeat each case with five documented seeds and distinguish observed variation from the exact theoretical cases.
deliverables: summary table and two diagnostic plots
acceptanceCriteria: The identical and opposite cases are constructed from the same base draw, not independent draws.
The theoretical sum variances are documented as 2, 4 and 0 respectively; sample discrepancies are reported rather than fabricated away.
An identical manifest reproduces the same arrays and summary values in the stated environment.

reviewPrompts: Why can two individually quiet quantities create a risky combined exposure?
What can a seeded simulation prove, and what can it not prove?

lessons.title: Estimation, confidence intervals and uncertain evidence
objectives: Separate sample variability from estimator uncertainty.
Construct and evaluate a confidence-interval procedure on known synthetic data.
Identify when dependence invalidates an independence-based uncertainty calculation.

topics.title: Estimators and sampling distributions
details: A statistic varies across repeated samples even when the data-generating process is unchanged.
Standard deviation describes observations; standard error describes an estimator.
Bias, variance and sample size should be discussed together.

topics.title: Interval interpretation
details: Frequentist coverage concerns the repeated-sampling procedure.
A realized 95% interval is not automatically a 95% posterior probability statement.
Bootstrap resampling requires assumptions about what can be resampled independently.

topics.title: Financial observations are not automatically independent
details: Serially correlated observations contain less independent information than their row count suggests.
Selection, missing data and regime change can dominate small standard errors.
Do not report a precise result without stating the model and sampling assumptions.

video.locator: Lecture 24: Classical Inference - II

reading.locator: Chapter 8 Estimation: 8.4 Sampling Distributions, 8.5 Standard Error, 8.6 Confidence Intervals

assignment.title: Measure interval coverage in an invented measurement process
instructions: Specify an independent normal generator with known mean and run 200 independent experiments, each with 100 observations.
Calculate a mean estimate, standard error and a stated confidence interval in each experiment; record whether it contains the known mean.
Repeat with serially correlated synthetic observations using the same naive interval and explain why this is a deliberately misspecified procedure.
acceptanceCriteria: Reported coverage is computed from stored experiment records and is not forced to equal the nominal percentage.
The independent and dependent generators, seeds and interval conventions are recorded.
The explanation distinguishes estimator uncertainty, simulation error and incorrect-model error.

reviewPrompts: Why is a small standard error not enough to trust a financial result?
How does interval coverage differ from the probability of a parameter under a Bayesian model?

modules.title: 2. Numerical Reliability and Statistical Model Discipline
modules.description: Apply mathematics to financial computation: numerical representations, stable linear algebra, root finding and the consequences of trying many hypotheses. Basic algebra and Python syntax remain in Common Foundation.

lessons.title: Prices, integer ticks, floating point and numerical error
objectives: Choose representations appropriate to prices, quantities and statistical calculations.
Distinguish rounding error, instability and an ill-conditioned problem.
Write unit-aware comparisons with justified tolerances.

topics.title: Exact discrete quantities
details: A tick is a declared price increment, not an arbitrary number of decimal places.
Integer ticks and integer quantities make matching invariants easier to specify.
Reject nonpositive quantities, off-tick prices and overflow-prone values explicitly.

topics.title: Approximate numerical quantities
details: Binary floating point cannot represent every decimal value exactly.
Cancellation can destroy meaningful digits when subtracting nearby quantities.
Conditioning belongs to a problem; stability describes how an algorithm handles it.

topics.title: Comparison policies
details: Use exact comparisons for discrete ledger invariants when their representation is exact.
Use scale-aware tolerances for model valuations and numerical solvers.
Store units and rounding policies alongside numerical outputs.

video.locator: Lecture 19 - Floating Point Arithmetic, public Segment 1

reading.locator: 1.1 Floating-point numbers; 1.2 Problems and conditioning; 1.4 Stability

assignment.title: Design an exact price codec and a numerical-error exhibit
instructions: Implement decimal-string-to-tick and tick-to-decimal-string conversion for fictional tick sizes 0.01 and 0.05 using exact decimal parsing.
Create 20 original accepted/rejected fixtures, including off-tick input and boundary values.
Separately demonstrate cancellation or accumulated floating-point error and document why a matching engine must not use that calculation as an order-priority key.
acceptanceCriteria: Accepted values round-trip exactly under the specified format.
Off-tick and invalid inputs fail with explicit reasons; they are not silently rounded into valid orders.
The chosen integer range and rounding/overflow policy are documented.

reviewPrompts: When is an epsilon comparison harmful rather than helpful?
Why does using more decimal digits not necessarily repair an unstable calculation?

lessons.title: Covariance matrices and stable least-squares calculations
objectives: Represent multiple synthetic measurements as vectors and matrices.
Explain covariance, positive semidefiniteness and collinearity.
Compare stable least-squares solving with a fragile normal-equations implementation.

topics.title: Financial matrix meaning
details: Rows can represent aligned sessions and columns comparable instrument measurements.
A covariance matrix needs a consistent sampling interval and missing-data policy.
Pairwise estimates from incompatible samples can undermine matrix properties.

topics.title: Regression as a numerical problem
details: Residuals are observed minus fitted values, not proof of causal effects.
Nearly redundant features make coefficients sensitive to small changes.
QR or a vetted least-squares solver avoids explicitly forming an inverse.

topics.title: Diagnostics
details: Inspect rank, residual magnitude and conditioning.
Evaluate predictive stability as well as coefficient values.
Document tolerances and distinguish exact arithmetic identities from floating-point checks.

video.locator: Lecture 21: Optimization with constraints; least-squares geometry and weighted least-squares portions

reading.locator: 3.2 The normal equations; 3.3 The QR factorization

assignment.title: Stress a small synthetic exposure regression
instructions: Generate 200 observations with two almost-collinear explanatory columns and a known linear response plus noise.
Compare a naive normal-equations solve with numpy.linalg.lstsq or QR, then perturb one column slightly.
Record coefficient changes, residual norms, matrix rank and conditioning without asserting that either coefficient represents causal exposure.
acceptanceCriteria: The comparison uses identical inputs and reports all solver warnings or failures.
A rank-deficient case is included and explicitly handled.
The report explains why similar fitted values may coexist with unstable individual coefficients.

reviewPrompts: Why can a small residual coexist with an unreliable coefficient?
Why prefer a linear solve or least-squares routine to explicitly inverting a matrix?

lessons.title: Root finding, discount curves and calibration failure
objectives: Express a fictional fixed-income calibration as a root problem.
Implement bounded stopping and error reporting.
Distinguish small residual, small update and accuracy of the inferred parameter.

topics.title: From cash flows to a residual
details: A calibration residual compares a model output with an input target.
The target and discount convention must be specified before solving.
A solution can be absent, nonunique or outside an economically allowed domain.

topics.title: Numerical methods
details: Bisection uses a sign-changing bracket; Newton uses local derivative information.
Newton can fail near a zero derivative or from a poor initial guess.
A maximum iteration count is a safety bound, not proof of convergence.

topics.title: Sensitivity and evidence
details: Report solver status, residual, iteration count and admissible parameter range.
Perturb targets to measure conditioning rather than hiding instability.
No result should look successful after a solver failure.

video.locator: Lecture 5: Inverses and Newton's Method; companion topic 1.6 The Newton Method

reading.locator: 4.1 The rootfinding problem; 4.3 Newton's method, including Convergence and Implementation

assignment.title: Build a bounded fictional bond-yield solver
instructions: Create five positive dated-cash-flow contracts and manufacture their prices from known annual effective rates.
Recover those rates using a bracketed method; implement Newton separately only as a comparison.
Include one impossible target, one failed bracket and one sensitivity experiment; return structured failure information instead of a default number.
acceptanceCriteria: All solvable fixtures recover the generating rate within a stated, scale-appropriate tolerance.
Invalid cases fail explicitly within a bounded number of iterations.
The report states cash-flow timing, rate convention and why a small price residual does not always imply a precise rate.

reviewPrompts: What evidence distinguishes a root from a solver that merely stopped?
Why should calibration code preserve the reason for failure?

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing and the cost of trying many ideas
objectives: Specify a null, alternative, statistic and testing family before evaluation.
Distinguish statistical significance from effect size and practical relevance.
Explain how repeated comparisons create false discoveries.

topics.title: Testing vocabulary
details: A p-value is computed under a specified null model; it is not the probability that the null is true.
A test statistic must be chosen before looking for an attractive result.
Power and false-positive control address different errors.

topics.title: Families of comparisons
details: The relevant family includes discarded candidates, not only the winner.
Bonferroni controls a family-wise error bound under its stated construction.
False discovery rate is a different objective and is introduced later in the research-audit module.

topics.title: Interpretation for research
details: Tiny effects can be statistically detectable yet economically irrelevant after costs.
Changing the hypothesis after seeing results changes the evidential story.
Reserve a genuinely untouched evaluation rather than repeatedly relabelling data as holdout.

video.locator: Lecture 25: Classical Inference - III

reading.locator: 9.1 Flipping Coins; 9.2 Testing a Difference in Means; read narrative only

assignment.title: Run a registered family of null comparisons
instructions: Generate 20 independent synthetic measurement streams with identical true means and prespecify 20 comparisons to a fixed known benchmark.
Evaluate unadjusted and Bonferroni-adjusted decisions over 100 seeded experiment families.
Keep every comparison, effect estimate and decision; explain the difference between per-test and family-wise error without promising an exact observed rate.
acceptanceCriteria: The declared comparison count matches the stored registry in every family.
The adjustment uses the full prespecified family rather than only significant comparisons.
No one favorable sample or corrected p-value is described as evidence of trading profitability.

reviewPrompts: Which abandoned experiments still count as research trials?
Why are corrected significance and useful effect size different questions?

modules.title: 3. Point-in-Time Financial Data and Time-Series Evaluation
modules.description: Bridge from data engineering to financial research through availability-time semantics, corporate actions, historical membership, chronological evaluation and reproducible snapshots. Correct data is necessary evidence infrastructure, not evidence of alpha.

lessons.title: Returns, corporate actions and historical instrument identity
objectives: Compute simple and log returns with their domain restrictions.
Explain the effect of dividends, splits and delistings on a historical panel.
Distinguish stable instrument identity from a mutable ticker label.

topics.title: Return conventions
details: Simple returns compound multiplicatively across periods; log returns are additive when defined.
A dividend-inclusive return differs from a price-only return.
Zero or negative prices require explicit handling before logarithms.

topics.title: Corporate actions
details: A split changes units and quoted price without creating wealth by itself.
Adjusted prices can be useful for some return calculations but inappropriate for historical price-level filters.
Delisted instruments and historical membership must not disappear from a retrospective universe.

topics.title: Data identity
details: Use an immutable instrument ID plus effective-dated ticker and corporate-action records.
Distinguish the event's effective time from the time the information became available.
Retain raw observations and the exact adjustment version used by a result.

video.locator: Lecture 1: Introduction, Financial Terms and Concepts; review returns and instrument terminology

reading.locator: Chapter 1 Return Calculations: 1.2.2 Simple returns, 1.2.3 Continuously compounded returns, and 1.4.4 Downloading financial data from the internet for adjusted-price discussion only

assignment.title: Create a tiny corporate-action correctness oracle
instructions: Invent 12 sessions for three fictional instruments, including a two-for-one split, a cash dividend, a ticker change and a delisting.
Store raw prices, stable IDs, action metadata and a documented historical membership table.
Hand-calculate four total-value/return checkpoints and compare them with a transformation; add a deliberately survivorship-biased view for diagnosis only.
acceptanceCriteria: The split changes share count but not the position's value absent another price movement.
The dividend is neither omitted nor counted twice.
The delisted instrument remains in the historical universe where eligible, and ticker changes do not create a new economic instrument.

reviewPrompts: When might adjusted prices leak information into a historical filter?
Why is today's list of surviving instruments unsuitable as a historical membership table?

lessons.title: Two clocks: event time, availability time and revisions
objectives: Write a point-in-time eligibility rule in plain language and code.
Resolve revisions, ties, exact matches and staleness explicitly.
Check an optimized as-of join against a slow knowledge-time oracle.

topics.title: What could have been known?
details: Event time says when something happened; availability time says when the simulated observer could first use it.
A reporting-period end is not a financial statement's publication time.
Later corrections must not rewrite what an earlier observer knew.

topics.title: Temporal contracts
details: Normalize timestamps to UTC while preserving source timezone and session metadata.
Define inclusive versus exclusive availability boundaries and deterministic tie breaking.
Distinguish missing, stale, rejected and revised observations instead of filling them silently.

topics.title: Reference implementation first
details: A slow scan that filters by eligible knowledge time is a useful oracle.
merge_asof needs sorted keys, grouping and the correct direction.
The accompanying replication lecture explains ordering and recorded inputs; it is not advertised as an as-of-join tutorial.

video.locator: Lecture 4: Primary-Backup Replication; focus ordered operations, recording nondeterministic inputs and repeatable state

reading.locator: Version Control for Data: Importance of Version Controlling Data, Challenges and Tools

assignment.title: Implement an availability-time join on a hand-auditable fixture
instructions: Create 30 quotes and eight disclosures for three fictional instruments with separate event and availability timestamps.
Include a revised disclosure, equal availability timestamps, a timezone offset and a stale quote; write a policy before implementing joins.
Produce ten snapshots using a simple scan and a pandas backward as-of join, then append a later revision and rerun earlier snapshots.
deliverables: optimized join and ten snapshot comparisons
acceptanceCriteria: No selected row has availability time after its snapshot time.
Appending future information leaves all earlier snapshot outputs unchanged.
Tie, exact-match and staleness cases match the oracle; tests fail for an intentionally event-time-only join.

questions.prompt: A result describes the quarter ending June 30 but is published July 25. Can a July 1 snapshot use it?
questions.answer: No, unless independently documented availability before July 1 exists; the reporting-period end is not publication time.
questions.explanation: Point-in-time eligibility follows actual knowledge availability, not the period being described.

reviewPrompts: What does a nearest-time join risk selecting?
Which revision policy would allow a historical snapshot to change, and why must that be explicit?

lessons.title: Time-series structure, baselines and rolling evaluation
objectives: Recognize serial dependence, nonstationarity and residual structure.
Construct chronological evaluation windows with a stated forecast horizon.
Compare a simple forecast with a defensible baseline without financial-return claims.

topics.title: Temporal structure
details: Autocorrelation measures association with lagged values, not causation.
Stationarity is a model assumption; trends and structural breaks can violate it.
Returns, price levels and quote spreads need not have the same time-series behavior.

topics.title: Forecast evaluation
details: A rolling origin never trains on observations after the forecast origin.
Fit preprocessing only on each training window.
For multi-step targets, exclude training labels that extend into the evaluation period.

topics.title: Diagnostics
details: Compare with a last-observation or training-mean baseline appropriate to the target.
Inspect residual autocorrelation, outliers and changing variance.
Forecast error is not an execution model or a measure of trading profitability.

Check a faster transformation for semantic equivalence before measuring it.

Data version, code version and dependency versions are separate identifiers.
Byte-identical exports require a canonical ordering and serialization convention.

A new corrected snapshot is a new version, not an undocumented overwrite.
Late information changes eligible future snapshots, not frozen prior knowledge.

Separate cold reads, parsing, computation and export time.
Performance reports include hardware and workload; no result is assumed in advance.

modules.title: 4. Market Microstructure and Deterministic Paper Exchange
modules.description: Learn exchange behavior through a fictional single-process limit-order book. Python is sufficient. This module builds correctness intuition, not a connection to an exchange or a claim of production low latency.

lessons.title: Quotes, trades, order types and matching policies
objectives: Explain the difference between a quote, an order, a trade and a position.
Trace price/FIFO priority under one explicitly defined venue model.
Specify cancellations, partial fills and rejection behavior without hidden defaults.

topics.title: Market vocabulary
details: The bid is a buying price and the ask a selling price; depth is available displayed quantity at price levels.
A trade changes executed quantities; a quote alone need not change a position.
Exchange, dealer and OTC arrangements have different mechanisms.

topics.title: One bounded matching policy
details: Use price priority, then FIFO within one price level, for the fictional venue.
Execute against the resting order's price under the chosen rule.
Define which order types are supported instead of implying every venue behaves identically.

topics.title: Lifecycle and safety
details: Received, rejected, resting, partially filled, filled and cancelled are distinct states.
Define cancellation of unknown or completed orders explicitly.
Self-trade prevention and auctions are real complications; the initial MVP must state whether they are excluded.

reading.locator: 2.5 Financial Markets

assignment.title: Write and hand-execute an original matching specification
instructions: Specify one fictional instrument, integer ticks, integer quantities and limit orders only.
Create 12 commands spanning two price levels, equal-price FIFO, a partial fill, cancellation and invalid input.
Hand-draw the book after each command and list every execution with resting/taking IDs and price; write explicit exclusions.
acceptanceCriteria: Each command has one defined accepted or rejected outcome.
All executions respect the chosen price/FIFO and resting-price rules.
The trace conserves each accepted order's original quantity across filled, cancelled and remaining quantities.

questions.prompt: Does observing an ask at a price establish that a simulated buy order would have filled there?
questions.answer: No. Arrival time, available size, queue state and the execution model still matter.
questions.explanation: Market observations do not automatically supply counterfactual fills for an unsubmitted order.

reviewPrompts: Which rule must be stated to determine an execution price?
Why should a cancelled order remain visible in an audit log even though it leaves the active book?

lessons.title: A simple matching engine and state invariants
objectives: Implement a deliberately simple reference matcher.
Choose data structures consistent with ordering and cancellation semantics.
Check invariants after every state transition.

topics.title: Reference before speed
details: A sorted list and per-level queue can be enough for a bounded prototype.
A separate order-ID index supports cancellation but must agree with active queues.
Queue removal and partial fills must not accidentally change time priority.

topics.title: Conservation and state consistency
details: Remaining quantities are never negative.
Executed quantity is identical for the two sides of a fill.
An order cannot simultaneously be terminal and active.

topics.title: Explicit error behavior
details: Duplicate command IDs and duplicate order IDs are different cases.
Validation happens before a command mutates the book.
Unsupported operations fail clearly rather than being treated as no-ops.

assignment.title: Implement a bounded Python reference exchange

Support new limit order and cancel commands, then emit typed accept/reject/fill events.
Add invariant checks after every command and extend the golden suite with at least eight original edge cases.

Rejected commands leave the book unchanged.
The ID index and level queues agree, terminal orders are absent from the active book, and all quantity checks pass.

reviewPrompts: What does the simplest implementation make easier to verify?
How can a cancellation bug violate FIFO without producing a negative quantity?

lessons.title: Sequenced command logs and deterministic replay
objectives: Define the authoritative input sequence for a paper exchange.
Replay accepted and rejected commands reproducibly.
Identify hidden nondeterminism beyond random-number seeds.

topics.title: Authoritative sequence
details: Assign one deterministic sequence number at the modeled acceptance boundary.
Preserve canonical inputs, policy version and rejection reasons.
Wall-clock arrival strings are not a substitute for an unambiguous processing order.

topics.title: Sources of nondeterminism
details: Unrecorded clocks, unordered iteration, randomness and concurrency can change behavior.
Replay must use recorded economic inputs, not re-query current external state.
A fixed seed alone does not define all nondeterministic inputs.

topics.title: Integrity and replay boundaries
details: Detect sequence gaps, duplicates and malformed records.
Define whether a truncated final record is recoverable or a fatal log error.
Compare canonical fills and state, not only a visual order-book display.

assignment.title: Make a paper engine replayable and detect damaged logs
instructions: Generate at most 5,000 commands independently of the matcher and store a canonical append-only log.
Replay the same log in three fresh processes and compare fill/state hashes.
Create separate gap, duplicate and truncated-record fixtures; define explicit failure or recovery behavior without inventing missing commands.
acceptanceCriteria: The three intact-log replays have identical canonical fills and final state.
Each damaged-log case produces the documented diagnostic and never silently reports a complete replay.
Replay does not access a broker, live feed, current clock for matching priority or mutable external dataset.

reviewPrompts: Which inputs must be recorded for a random seed to be meaningful?
Why is identical final depth weaker evidence than identical fills and final order state?

lessons.title: Golden traces, randomized testing and reproducible failures
objectives: Compare an alternative implementation against a simple oracle.
Generate bounded stateful command sequences with reproducible seeds.
Reduce a failure to a short explanatory counterexample.

topics.title: Independent evidence
details: A faster implementation and its reference should not share the same matching loop.
Golden examples test known outcomes; invariants test broader properties.
A regression test can preserve an existing bug unless its expected output is independently justified.

topics.title: Stateful generation
details: Include both valid and invalid commands and preserve the generator seed.
Generate cancellations, duplicate IDs and partial-fill chains, not only easy insertions.
Shrinking or manual reduction makes a long failing history understandable.

topics.title: Concurrency boundary
details: Keep authoritative matching single-sequenced until ordering semantics are proven.
Parallel input generation is not permission to reorder accepted commands.
Record failure details explicitly instead of suppressing exceptions in a benchmark.

instructions: Write a second small matcher representation and compare it with the reference on 50 seeded histories of at most 200 commands each.

Find a failing history, reduce it to a short case and restore the correct implementation; retain the regression test, not the defect.

Restored code agrees on fills, rejects and final order state for every stored history.
The reduced trace is sufficient to explain the violated invariant; passing test counts are measured, not prefilled.

reviewPrompts: Why can two implementations agreeing still be insufficient proof?
What makes a minimized failure more valuable than a large random log?

modules.title: 5. Research Design, Honest Backtesting and Experiment Audits
modules.description: Evaluate research procedures on synthetic data, not proposed real-money strategies. Separate statistical evidence, implementation correctness, execution assumptions and economic interpretation. A paper backtest or paper-trading result is not proof of tradable profitability.

lessons.title: Falsifiable hypotheses, baselines and preregistered decisions
objectives: Turn an informal financial-data idea into a bounded testable question.
Separate exploratory analysis from confirmatory evaluation.
Write stop, revise and reject criteria before seeing held-out results.

topics.title: Research question versus attractive chart
details: A hypothesis states what should change, under what information and compared with which baseline.
An economic explanation can motivate a test without establishing causality.
A negative result can be useful if the protocol and evidence are complete.

topics.title: Decisions before evaluation
details: Define the target, observation unit, horizon, metric, candidate family and allowed preprocessing.
Declare which data are exploratory and which evaluation is frozen.
Specify missing-data, outlier and revision policies rather than choosing them after seeing results.

topics.title: Communication
details: Report assumptions, effect estimates and uncertainty together.
Keep a trial register, including abandoned variants and reasons for changes.
Do not treat a market-efficiency lecture or a causal story as endorsement of an actionable strategy.

instructions: Specify a fictional hypothesis that larger message bursts are associated with more stale quotes; do not frame it as a trading strategy.

Both candidates and the baseline are reported even if the preferred explanation fails.
Any protocol deviation is dated and labelled exploratory, not silently incorporated into a confirmatory claim.

When does a new analysis require a new evaluation dataset?

lessons.title: A backtest clock that respects available information
objectives: Specify event ordering between observations, decisions, simulated orders and fills.
Prevent future labels or same-bar information from entering earlier decisions.
Distinguish an event-driven engine's guarantees from its remaining assumptions.

topics.title: Simulation chronology
details: A bar's closing value is not known at that bar's opening time.
Information receipt, decision time, order eligibility and simulated fill time are separate boundaries.
Explicit latency and session rules are more honest than assuming immediate execution.

topics.title: Training and evaluation
details: Fit feature transforms and parameters only within their declared training partition.
Purge overlapping training labels when their outcome windows cross an evaluation boundary.
Repeatedly inspecting holdout results converts them into development information.

topics.title: What a paper simulation does not prove
details: A deterministic engine can still use incorrect data or implausible fills.
Historical quotes do not expose every counterfactual queue position.
The output is a result under assumptions, not a promise of live performance.

assignment.title: Build a time-boundary audit simulator
instructions: Create 40 synthetic sessions and a fixed, prespecified inventory-adjustment schedule unrelated to future prices.
Log observation availability, decision, order and fill timestamps; enforce a declared next-eligible-event fill rule.
Introduce an exercise-only same-bar-close leak and an overlapping-label leak, then write tests that detect both and restore the valid implementation.

acceptanceCriteria: Every decision can be reconstructed from information available at its decision time.
Every fill occurs no earlier than the declared eligibility boundary and respects the simulated session rules.
Both intentional leaks are detected; no paper result is labelled a profitable or deployable strategy.

reviewPrompts: Why does an event-driven API not automatically eliminate look-ahead bias?
Which timestamp determines when a feature becomes usable?

lessons.title: Spreads, fees, slippage, impact and capacity assumptions
objectives: Separate accounting costs from uncertainty about execution.
Represent partial fills, borrow constraints and liquidity limits explicitly.
Run a cost-sensitivity analysis without optimizing a trading strategy.

topics.title: Costs are not one constant
details: Fees and commissions differ from spread crossing and modeled market impact.
Financing, stock-borrow availability and borrow charges can affect feasibility.
A mark-to-mid valuation is not necessarily an executable liquidation value.

topics.title: Execution uncertainty
details: Queue position, arrival time and displayed size limit plausible fills.
Historical depth is not a guarantee that the same liquidity remains available to a hypothetical order.
Capacity requires considering scale and market interaction, not multiplying a small simulation linearly.

topics.title: Sensitivity and honest reporting
details: Label every cost/impact assumption as synthetic or externally sourced.
Compare fixed execution schedules under different assumptions without cherry-picking the cheapest model.
Never calibrate an optimistic fill model solely to improve reported returns.

Evaluate three declared fee/spread assumptions and a separate depth-limited partial-fill case.
Include an unavailable-borrow rejection for a short-order example and report all unfilled quantities and model limitations.

No simulated fill exceeds eligible quantity or the declared depth limit.
Borrow-unavailable orders are rejected, and every reported result identifies its fill and cost model rather than claiming observed market performance.

reviewPrompts: Which costs are deterministic inputs and which depend on hypothetical market behavior?
Why is zero commission not equivalent to zero transaction cost?

lessons.title: Selection bias, experiment registries and overfitting audits
objectives: Explain why selecting the best backtest on noise can manufacture an attractive result.
Distinguish family-wise error, false discovery rate and out-of-sample deterioration.
Audit a full experiment history rather than a single winning chart.

topics.title: Selection changes interpretation
details: The maximum result across many candidates is not distributed like a single prespecified test.
Feature, universe, window and cost-model choices all contribute to the search.
An ordinary holdout loses independence if it repeatedly influences the next candidate.

topics.title: Complete experiment records
details: Store candidate definitions, dataset hashes, split boundaries, seeds and all outcomes.
Record abandoned and failed runs, not only successful training jobs.
A research approval decision must explain limitations and rejected alternatives.

topics.title: Evidence boundaries
details: Multiple-testing adjustments do not fix leakage, survivorship or unrealistic execution.
Paper trading adds operational evidence but does not establish real-money profitability.
LLM-generated explanations and strategies are hypotheses, not independently validated alpha.

acceptanceCriteria: Exactly 100 candidate definitions are present, including failed or rejected evaluations with reasons.

What does an FDR statement control, and what does it leave unaddressed?

lessons.title: Cash, positions, marks and reconciliation
objectives: Distinguish executed trades from position and cash balances.
Define a valuation convention and separate cash movement from mark changes.
Reconcile an event ledger with an independently calculated ending state.

topics.title: Economic state
details: A fill creates changes to cash and position under the project's simplified settlement convention.
A mark is a valuation input, not necessarily an executable trade price.
Deposits, withdrawals and fees must not be mislabeled as investment returns.

topics.title: Accounting conventions
details: Declare cost-basis and rounding policies before reporting realized and unrealized components.
Keep one fictional currency initially; do not silently mix FX conversion assumptions.
A missing or stale price should produce an explicit incomplete-valuation status.

topics.title: Reconciliation
details: Compare event-derived balances with an independent control calculation.
Repeated event IDs must not post balances twice.
Corrections need auditable reversals or versioned replacement policy, not hidden edits.

Duplicate delivery does not double-post, and the correction remains traceable.
A missing/stale mark never becomes zero silently; the valuation report identifies the affected exposure and its status.

Why should a risk dashboard distinguish an unavailable mark from a zero-valued position?

lessons.title: Diversification, covariance and minimum-variance models
objectives: Calculate portfolio variance with consistent units and horizon.
Solve a small fully invested minimum-variance exercise.
Demonstrate sensitivity to estimated covariance rather than trusting precise weights.

topics.title: Risk aggregation
details: Portfolio variance depends on both individual variances and cross-covariances.
Diversification is limited when exposures share the same shocks.
A fully invested constraint does not automatically mean long-only or unlevered.

topics.title: Numerical portfolio construction
details: Use matrix methods with explicit symmetry, rank and conditioning checks.
Solve the linear system rather than blindly forming an inverse.
Distinguish an optimizer's numerical solution from a reliable estimate of future risk.

topics.title: Estimation uncertainty
details: Short histories and structural change make covariance estimates unstable.
Regularization or shrinkage imposes assumptions that must be recorded.
Sensitivity analysis is part of the result, not an optional footnote.

Add a singular matrix case and report failure or documented regularization separately from the original model.

Weights satisfy the specified budget constraint and risk is computed from the same covariance convention.

What risk is omitted by describing diversification only in terms of the number of instruments?

lessons.title: Constraints, factor exposure and infeasible portfolio requests
objectives: Express budget, position and concentration limits as explicit constraints.
Interpret a small exposure matrix and distinguish modeled factors from causal drivers.
Handle infeasible optimization requests without returning misleading defaults.

topics.title: A model is a contract
details: Specify long-only, gross/net exposure, per-instrument caps and group limits.
Turnover and transaction costs can change the feasible or preferred solution.
Every target must use the same horizon and units as its inputs.

topics.title: Factor interpretation
details: Factor exposure aggregates position weights and assumed loadings.
CAPM beta is a model-based sensitivity estimate, not a guarantee of future behavior.
Changing the benchmark, sample or frequency changes estimated exposures.

topics.title: Optimization status
details: Distinguish optimal, inaccurate, infeasible and failed statuses.
Validate returned weights independently of the solver's status message.
Never substitute equal weights or zeros and label that a successful constrained solution.

Factor exposures equal the independent matrix calculation.
The impossible request returns an explicit infeasible outcome, not an apparently valid default allocation or an investment recommendation.

What information is needed to compare two reported beta estimates?

lessons.title: VaR, tail loss, stress scenarios and model limitations
objectives: State a loss sign convention, horizon and quantile convention.
Distinguish a quantile threshold from the severity of losses beyond it.
Create scenario and reconciliation reports without claiming regulatory compliance.

topics.title: Risk measures
details: VaR is a loss quantile under a stated model and horizon, not a worst-case bound.
An empirical tail average describes loss severity beyond a selected tail boundary.
Expected shortfall conventions for discrete data and ties must be stated; the lesson is not a Basel implementation.

topics.title: Stress and liquidity
details: Apply explicit joint price/rate shocks and consider stale marks or missing liquidity.
Stress scenarios are assumptions, not forecasts with known probabilities.
Historical samples may omit the adverse states that matter most.

topics.title: Model-risk communication
details: Report sample size, estimation period and scaling assumptions.
Do not apply square-root-of-time scaling without checking its assumptions.
Credit, counterparty, operational and market risks are related but not interchangeable.

Apply three invented joint shocks to a small paper portfolio and reconcile scenario valuations to position-level calculations.

acceptanceCriteria: The two fixtures have the intended identical VaR but different worst-five averages.
Every output names the horizon, units, sign convention and empirical tail convention.
Scenario totals equal their position-level components; no metric is described as a maximum possible loss or regulatory certification.

How should a report describe a stress scenario's probability when none was estimated?

lessons.title: Pricing lane: Monte Carlo uncertainty and the calculus boundary
objectives: Separate Monte Carlo sampling error from discretization and model error.
Compare a simulated payoff expectation with a small exact reference.
Explain what additional stochastic-process study is needed before using continuous-time formulas.

topics.title: Discrete stochastic models first
details: A random walk is an explicit sequence of random increments.
Independent simulated paths provide a sampling distribution for a payoff estimate.
A seeded estimate can be reproducible and still inaccurate.

topics.title: Three error sources
details: Sampling error comes from finite paths.
Discretization error comes from replacing a continuous-time model with time steps.
Model error remains even if numerical and sampling errors are negligible.

topics.title: Lane-specific extension
details: Brownian motion, martingales, Ito calculus, stochastic differential equations and risk-neutral measures require a dedicated mathematical sequence.
A short lecture preview is not evidence of stochastic-calculus proficiency.
Do not import continuous-time hedging conclusions into a discrete paper simulator without its assumptions.

assignment.title: Compare exact path enumeration with Monte Carlo
instructions: Define an original symmetric ten-step random walk and a bounded terminal payoff, then enumerate all 1,024 paths to obtain an exact expectation.
Estimate the same expectation from 5,000 independent simulated paths for each of 100 documented seeds.
Calculate standard errors and interval coverage against the exact value; explain why this checks the numerical experiment rather than a financial market model.
acceptanceCriteria: The enumerator includes every path with its correct probability and serves as an independent reference.
Coverage and errors are measured from all runs, not forced to a desired value.
The report does not call this discrete exercise a validated continuous-time pricing or hedging system.

reviewPrompts: Which error shrinks by simulating more paths, and which does not?
Why is an exact answer under a wrong model still potentially misleading?

lessons.title: Research lane: timestamp-safe financial ML against simple baselines
objectives: Build a small supervised experiment with financial information-timing constraints.
Compare regularization/model complexity against a frozen simple baseline.
Audit preprocessing, label overlap and distribution shift before interpreting model quality.

topics.title: Financial features and labels
details: Features must be observable at the decision timestamp, including their revision state.
A future target is allowed as a label, not as an input feature.
Forecasting a spread or volatility quantity does not by itself establish executable alpha.

topics.title: Model comparison
details: Start with a training-mean or last-observation baseline and a small regularized model.
Choose hyperparameters on chronological development data and inspect regime-specific errors.
Deep learning and GPU training are optional later specializations, not automatic improvements.

topics.title: AI-assisted work
details: LLM-generated code and explanations require the same correctness and leakage review as human-authored work.
Pretrained-model data cutoffs can contaminate retrospective financial tasks.
Never label an AI-generated hypothesis as validated alpha without independent evidence.

assignment.title: Evaluate a small synthetic future-spread model
instructions: Generate 1,000 synthetic quote observations with a known regime change and a future-spread label.
Use ordered 600/200/200 training, validation and untouched test partitions; compare a baseline, ridge model and at most one small tree.
Add an intentionally leaked future column only in a diagnostic copy, prove the feature-availability audit rejects it, and report all valid models without converting results into trading advice.
acceptanceCriteria: Scaling, feature selection and hyperparameters use only the allowed development partitions.
The future-feature diagnostic fails explicitly and is absent from the final feature set.
Results include the simple baseline and regime-level errors; no simulated forecast metric is called profitability, alpha or production readiness.

reviewPrompts: Why can a pretrained model leak historical knowledge even when your local split is chronological?
What evidence would justify a more complex model than the baseline?

modules.title: 8. Controlled Delivery, Recovery and Auditable Evidence
modules.description: Professional practice means controlled, reviewable behavior, not a claim that a student prototype is production-ready. This module does not require the optional C++, stochastic-calculus or ML lanes. Work remains local and synthetic.

lessons.title: Paper-system guardrails, incident decisions and responsible use
objectives: Place validation and risk controls at explicit state-transition boundaries.
Define safe failure behavior and operator actions.
Distinguish a useful controls reference from legal or regulatory certification.

topics.title: Pre-change controls
details: Check instrument validity, tick/quantity rules, notional/position limits and mark freshness before accepting a state-changing action.
The same checks must apply to repeated, restored and manually initiated commands.
A rejected command must have an auditable reason and no hidden state mutation.

topics.title: Operational response
details: Define a kill or pause mode, the state it affects and who may reset it in the prototype.
Monitor repeated rejects, missing sequences, reconciliation failures and stale inputs.
Preserve incident inputs and recovery evidence instead of treating an alert as the entire response.

topics.title: Responsible boundaries
details: Know that spoofing, wash trading and misuse of confidential information are not legitimate learning goals.
Use synthetic fixtures or separately verified licensed data; do not publish employer data or credentials.
FINRA is a US example; actual India-specific SEBI/exchange obligations require a separate current professional review before any real deployment.

assignment.title: Implement and exercise a paper-system control matrix
instructions: Define six controls for a fictional account, including stale mark, maximum order quantity, maximum position, duplicate command, sequence integrity and a pause mode.
Create at least 12 normal/boundary/failure scenarios and record expected state changes and operator response.
Implement the controls around a small local command processor and write one incident report from an intentionally triggered reconciliation failure.
acceptanceCriteria: Every rejected action leaves economic state unchanged and emits a specific reason.
Pause/reset behavior is deterministic and testable; replay does not bypass controls.
The report explicitly disclaims real brokerage access, legal certification and production readiness.

reviewPrompts: What does a kill switch stop, and what state still needs reconciliation afterward?
Why is a list of alerts not the same as an incident-response procedure?

lessons.title: Consistent snapshots, recovery and schema evolution
objectives: Bind a snapshot to an exact log position and policy version.
Recover book, cash and positions without double-applying events.
Reject or migrate incompatible snapshots explicitly.

topics.title: Snapshot completeness
details: Record the last included sequence number, schema version, policy version and content hash.
Economic state includes outstanding orders, balances and processed-command identity where needed.
A snapshot that omits deduplication state can become incorrect after a retry.

topics.title: Crash boundaries
details: Define what is durable before acknowledging a command.
A recovery procedure must distinguish logged, applied and acknowledged work.
A single-process design still needs an explicit atomicity and truncation policy.

topics.title: Evolution and auditability
details: Use versioned migrations or fail with an actionable incompatibility error.
Validate snapshot integrity before restoring state.
Never silently combine a snapshot from one policy version with events interpreted under another.

video.locator: Lecture 7: Fault Tolerance: Raft (2); persistent logs, crash/restart, snapshots and replay

reading.locator: Runtime testing; Acceptance and Regression Testing, especially Limitations of Regression Testing; apply these checks to the recovery contract

assignment.title: Prove snapshot-plus-tail equivalence at crash boundaries
instructions: Create a self-contained two-instrument, one-currency state fixture with at most 10,000 paper events and processed-command IDs.
Take snapshots at three log positions and compare restored-plus-tail state with a clean full replay.
Inject five documented crashes or corruptions around log append, state application, acknowledgement and snapshot writing; include one incompatible schema version.
acceptanceCriteria: Each intact snapshot-plus-tail run equals the full replay for fills, active orders, cash, positions and deduplication state.
No acknowledged event is silently lost and no redelivered event double-posts under the stated durability contract.
Corrupt or incompatible snapshots fail explicitly or follow a documented tested migration; there is no success-shaped fallback.

reviewPrompts: Why does a snapshot need a log position as well as a timestamp?
Which omitted state can make recovery appear correct until the first retry?

lessons.title: Workload design, observability and honest performance reports
objectives: Separate latency, throughput, correctness and recovery objectives.
Build a reproducible bounded benchmark with interpretable instrumentation.
Report results and uncertainty without inventing thresholds or speedups.

topics.title: Representative workload
details: Declare command mix, cancellation rate, active book depth, instrument count and input size.
A tiny all-insert workload is not equivalent to a cancellation-heavy matching workload.
Distinguish warm-up, steady state, parsing, matching, persistence and output costs.

topics.title: Measurement discipline
details: Record hardware, OS, runtime/compiler, dependency versions and exact commands.
Use a suitable monotonic duration clock and report units and aggregation conventions.
Instrument queue/backlog and reject/reconciliation counts without hiding failures.

topics.title: Claims and limits
details: A benchmark is evidence for its stated setup, not a universal capacity guarantee.
Tail latency needs enough samples and a stated percentile estimator.
Do not claim improvement unless baseline and alternative are equivalent and actually measured.

video.locator: Lecture 10: Measurement and Timing

reading.locator: General guidance and good practice for testing: Test Realistic Cases and Document the tests and how to run them; Reproducible Environments

assignment.title: Publish a reproducible local paper-system benchmark
instructions: Define three synthetic workloads: mostly resting orders, frequent cancellations and frequent crossings; cap each at 50,000 commands.
Run correctness checks first, then measure at least five runs per workload with an explicit warm-up policy.
Report raw samples, throughput, selected latency summaries, rejected-command counts and recovery time for one bounded snapshot restore; no target number is supplied.
acceptanceCriteria: All performance runs refer to a passing semantic-equivalence result and exact dataset/configuration hashes.
The report preserves raw measurements, failed runs and outliers with explanations.
No benchmark value, percentile, speedup or service-level claim is initialized before measurement.

reviewPrompts: Which workload variable could reverse the apparent winner between two designs?
Why is reporting only the fastest run misleading?

lessons.title: Independent review, reproducible handoff and evidence-based claims
objectives: Assemble a reviewable evidence package for one bounded project.
Distinguish historical self-report, reconstructed functionality and newly measured evidence.
Demonstrate a normal workflow and an intentional failure without exposing private data.

topics.title: Review package
details: Include scope, architecture, state/data contracts, source provenance and dependency versions.
Connect each requirement to a test, a result and a known limitation.
Document rejected alternatives and operational assumptions, not only the final design.

topics.title: Independent reproduction
details: A clean process must recreate fixtures, run tests and rebuild the reported artifacts.
Review command ordering and races even when tests pass.
Use an audit checklist to distinguish a missing result from a failed result.

topics.title: Honest portfolio presentation
details: A projects are current reconstructions of user-reported completed college work; their reconstruction status starts incomplete.
B projects are future builds and receive no completion date or claimed result before implementation.
Do not publish employer data/code, private credentials or claims of real trading profitability.

assignment.title: Produce and independently audit one paper-project release
instructions: Choose one project mapping below and assemble a release candidate using only its completed, actually measured artifacts; leave missing items visibly incomplete.
Have a peer, or a documented second clean execution by you, follow the setup without relying on notebook memory or unstated files.
Record a short local demo of a normal path and a deliberate failure, then write a claim-by-claim evidence table and a repair list.
deliverables: README, architecture diagram and setup/test commands
normal/failure demo, measured report and claim-evidence table
acceptanceCriteria: A clean execution reproduces the stated fixtures and test results or records specific unresolved blockers.
Every numerical claim points to raw measured evidence and its environment.
The release contains no employer/private assets, brokerage credentials, fabricated completion dates or alpha claims; incomplete milestones remain incomplete.

reviewPrompts: Which claims can the reviewer independently reproduce today?
How should the project be described when its historical version is user-reported but the reconstruction is unfinished?

projectMappings.scope: Reconstruct a bounded Python prototype with one fictional instrument and fewer than 100,000 generated commands. No live broker/feed, professional latency claim or required C++.

milestones.title: 1. Specify price/FIFO behavior and independent golden fixtures
deliverables: At least 20 original golden scenarios, including partial fill, cancel and invalid input
acceptanceCriteria: Every command has a defined result and execution-price policy.
Fixtures account for original, filled, cancelled and remaining quantities.
The MVP explicitly excludes real connectivity and unsupported venue features.

milestones.title: 2. Deliver a local order-entry, matching and replay slice
deliverables: Append-only canonical command log and replay command
acceptanceCriteria: A scripted normal workflow produces the hand-calculated fills and book.
A fresh replay reproduces canonical fills and final state.
The application runs from its own fixtures without another portfolio project's service.

milestones.title: 3. Establish invariants, reference equivalence and failure behavior
acceptanceCriteria: Seeded histories agree with an independently structured simple reference.
Rejected commands leave economic state unchanged.
Damaged logs fail or recover exactly according to a documented policy, never silently.

milestones.title: 4. Publish a reproducible demo and measured bounded workload
deliverables: README, dependency versions and test/start commands
Hardware-labelled throughput/latency report with raw results
acceptanceCriteria: A clean process reproduces the evidence package.
Every reported benchmark was actually measured on the documented workload.
Resume/demo language says paper simulation and reconstruction; no profit or professional-trading claim is made.

projectMappings.scope: Reconstruct three fictional instruments over 20 sessions using pandas, DuckDB and local tests. Generate quotes and disclosures independently, with event/availability times.

milestones.title: 1. Define temporal policies and a hand-written oracle
deliverables: Revision, tie, staleness and timezone policies
Synthetic generator and ten hand-audited snapshot fixtures
acceptanceCriteria: Event time and availability time are distinct fields with stated semantics.
A disclosure-period end is never substituted for its publication time.
Expected outputs cover stale, tied, revised and timezone-shifted cases.

milestones.title: 2. Build backward availability joins and snapshot exports
deliverables: Reference scan and pandas/DuckDB processing path
Quote age, spread, source ID and revision metadata
acceptanceCriteria: No snapshot selects unavailable future information.
All output values can be traced to eligible source records.
The workbench runs independently without the paper exchange or paid market data.

milestones.title: 3. Prove revision stability and optimized-join equivalence
acceptanceCriteria: Appending a later disclosure cannot change an earlier frozen snapshot.
Ties, exact matches and staleness follow the declared policy.
Optimized outputs equal the oracle, including lineage and missing-status fields.

milestones.title: 4. Deliver a correction demo and reproducible correctness/performance report
deliverables: Measured reference/optimized comparison and known limitations
acceptanceCriteria: Repeated same-version runs reproduce canonical output hashes.

projectMappings.scope: Planned standalone Python-first build: five fictional instruments, five prefunded accounts, one currency and initially at most 50,000 commands. Add a sequenced cash/position ledger, snapshots and reconciliation. No shorts, margin, real settlement or brokerage connection in the MVP; optional C++ is not required.

milestones.title: 1. Specify global sequencing and economic invariants
deliverables: Multi-instrument command, account and ledger schemas
Atomic fill-posting, prefunding and fee-account policies
acceptanceCriteria: Every modeled event has an unambiguous sequence and accounting effect.
The design states how available versus reserved cash/positions are calculated.
The standalone scope is meaningfully larger than A and does not present the same application twice under different names.

milestones.title: 2. Deliver matching-to-ledger posting with visible balances
deliverables: Deterministic event log and full replay
acceptanceCriteria: Each fill posts its cash and position effects exactly once.

deliverables: Independent cash, position and fill reconciliation report
acceptanceCriteria: Snapshot-plus-tail state equals full replay across all instruments and accounts.

Cash transfers, modeled fees and position transfers reconcile under the stated closed-system conventions.

milestones.title: 4. Review controls and publish a measured release candidate
deliverables: Measured workload, recovery and limitations report
acceptanceCriteria: Clean reproduction covers the sequenced matcher, ledger, snapshot and reconciliation path.

The release remains labelled a paper prototype without real-market profitability or production-certification claims.

projectMappings.scope: Planned standalone platform for five fictional instruments and up to 100 sessions with at most 100,000 generated rows. Version source data, availability-time revisions, schemas, policy definitions and research snapshots. Forecasting/strategy optimization is outside the MVP.

milestones.title: 1. Specify versioned knowledge-time contracts and lineage
deliverables: Immutable source/revision model and stable instrument IDs
Snapshot manifest and policy/schema version definitions
Independent oracle fixtures and licensing/provenance policy
acceptanceCriteria: Effective time, availability time and ingestion/audit time are not conflated.
Correction, supersession, membership and tie policies have explicit examples.
No employer data or unlicensed market-data redistribution is needed.

milestones.title: 2. Deliver an ingest-to-snapshot vertical slice
deliverables: Versioned as-of snapshot API or local CLI
acceptanceCriteria: A versioned snapshot can be regenerated from its manifest without ambient notebook state.
Invalid rows remain traceable with reasons rather than disappearing.
The project runs independently with its own generator and fixtures.

milestones.title: 3. Prove temporal correctness through corrections and backfills
deliverables: Boundary, revision, duplicate-batch and schema tests
Bounded backfill/rebuild and old-version immutability evidence
acceptanceCriteria: Later information never leaks into earlier knowledge-time snapshots.
Duplicate ingestion is idempotent and corrected rebuilds equal the declared clean reference.
Optimization preserves selected source IDs, revision versions and stale/missing statuses.

milestones.title: 4. Ship a reproducible research-data release and audit
deliverables: Rebuild/correction demo and clean setup instructions
Measured join/backfill report and an independent manifest audit
acceptanceCriteria: A reviewer can rebuild two distinct snapshot versions and explain their differences.
All timing claims have raw evidence and workload/environment details.
Claims are limited to data correctness/reproducibility, not investment advantage or validated alpha.

projectMappings.scope: Planned independent local service for five fictional accounts, three equity-like instruments and one fixed-cash-flow instrument, with one currency and declared valuation conventions. milestones.title: 1. Specify valuation, accounting and exposure conventions
deliverables: Cost-basis, discounting, rounding and correction rules

deliverables: Independent balance reconciliation and explicit incomplete-status outputs
acceptanceCriteria: Aggregate reports equal their position/account components.
Duplicate deliveries do not double-post balances.

deliverables: At least three documented joint stress scenarios
Correction, snapshot recovery and reconciliation-failure tests
acceptanceCriteria: The selected valuation fixtures match hand calculations within justified tolerances.

Recovery preserves accounting, source versions and event deduplication state.

deliverables: Scope/architecture document and clean run commands
Measured workload report, risk limitations and claim-evidence table
acceptanceCriteria: A reviewer can reproduce the fixtures, reports and intentional failure.
All benchmarks and result counts are measured after implementation.

limitations: Every module, lesson, assignment, project and milestone starts with status not_started. No current reconstruction, build, benchmark or proficiency result is initialized as completed.

Common Foundation supplies basic Python, SQL, Git, Linux, elementary mathematics and testing. It is a shared starting path, not a concatenation of these advanced modules. No undefined cross-track prerequisite IDs are introduced here.

Module 7 is optional and is not required by the professional module or project mappings. C++ fundamentals alone do not establish advanced C++ capability; stochastic calculus, derivatives modeling, deep learning, FPGA and low-latency networking are lane-dependent.

Estimated minutes include selected lectures, readings, the original bounded assignment and review for someone with Common Foundation readiness. They are planning estimates, not lecture durations or guarantees. Additional remediation and the complete project milestones can take substantially longer.

Every assignment is original and uses independently generated fictional data. Do not copy textbook/exam/platform problem statements or solution text. Do not substitute employer data, private reports, credentials or unlicensed market-data archives.

No PDFs or recordings were downloaded during this curriculum task. All downloadUrl fields are null; a later book-library workflow must independently verify an official download route and its exact applicable rights before fetching or hosting a copy.

Only The Turing Way text and Open Data Structures are marked redistribution permitted, subject to attribution, source/license links, change notices and third-party exceptions. Text, code, slides, images and recordings can have different licenses.

Think Stats, current OpenStax Principles of Finance and the Saylor adaptation have verified noncommercial/share-alike conditions but remain link-only here pending deployment-specific review. OpenStax also states additional AI-ingestion restrictions; this file contains original curriculum metadata and links, not book ingestion or chapter copies.

FNC's exercise license is not a whole-book license. Zivot, FPP3 and ISLP remain link-only because no applicable book-hosting grant was established. Authorized free access does not authorize mirroring, excerpt libraries or unrestricted reuse.

ISLP chapter titles/page ranges were verified through Springer-deposited Crossref metadata and official author resources, not downloaded chapter bodies. Its author access route may involve Google Drive quota or sign-in behavior that was not tested.

Video verification establishes official public locators, titles and selected descriptions/captions, not playback availability in every region. The historical MIT 6.824 archive worked over HTTP; HTTPS failed. Do not submit credentials to that archive. Computational Thinking Floating Point uses only public Segment 1.

Some videos are complementary theory rather than end-to-end finance tutorials: replication supports recorded-input determinism; performance lectures support data-structure/measurement reasoning. Availability-time joins, ledger conventions and paper controls are taught through explicit original lessons and official supplementary documentation.

Older lectures/books remain useful for mathematical foundations but their historical fees, technology examples, market commentary and regulations are not current operational facts. FPP3's online update was September 16, 2026; edition-specific locators are recorded rather than invented timestamps.

Think Stats uses a less strict confidence-interval interpretation in one passage; the lessons explicitly teach repeated-sampling frequentist coverage rather than equating it with posterior parameter probability.

The expected-shortfall exercise uses a clearly stated empirical worst-tail convention and is not a production or regulatory implementation. The BIS source is a historical 2016 announcement, and FINRA 15-09 is a US controls example, not a complete current Indian legal checklist.

No real brokerage connections, paid data service, market orders, investment recommendations or alpha/profit claims are required or authorized. Paper backtests and paper trading are not proof of tradable profitability. AI/LLM assistance does not validate financial hypotheses.

All numerical performance outputs must be measured after implementation and linked to raw artifacts. Acceptance criteria specify correctness properties and bounded workloads, not invented throughput, latency, Sharpe ratios, accuracy or hiring outcomes.

Each portfolio project must run independently with its own fixtures, setup and evidence. Reusing learned ideas is encouraged, but one application must not be counted twice under different project names. No account, repository or shared-browser changes are part of this research handoff.
